en: The Jātaka:
The Collection of Twenty, Chapter on Mātaṅga.
10. The Campeyya Jātaka:
“Who is it that shines like lightning, like a herb among the stars?”
"You are a goddess or a gandhabba;
I do not think you are human.
"I am neither a goddess nor a gandhabba."
"I am not human, Great King;
I am a Nāga maiden, venerable sir,
and I have come here for a certain purpose."
“Your mind is distracted and your faculties are agitated;
streams of water flow from your eyes.
What have you lost? Or what are you longing for?”
“A woman has come here; pray, tell us who she is.
“O Lord of Men, that which people call ‘the serpent of fierce heat’ and ‘the Naga,’ they call him so.”
“A man seeking a livelihood seized him;
release him from bondage, for he is my husband.
“How indeed has he come to possess such strength and vigor?”
It has come into the hands of a beggar;
tell me that matter, O Naga maiden:
how may we recognize the Naga who has been taken?
“A Naga could reduce even a city to ashes,
for he is endowed with such power and energy;
yet a Naga who honors the Dhamma— ”
Therefore, exerting himself, he practices austerity.
O King, on the fourteenth and the fifteenth day,
the Naga king gathers at the crossroads.
“A man seeking a livelihood has seized her;
release her from bondage, for she is my wife.
“Sixteen thousand women...”
Even that woman, adorned with earrings of supreme jewels,
who dwelt in a house by the water, has gone to him for refuge.
Release him by means of the Dhamma, not by force—
with a village, a coin, or a hundred cows—
let the snake go forth with its body cast off.
“May he who seeks merit be released from bondage.
“I release you by means of the Dhamma, not by force—
with a village, a coin, or a hundred cows.”
Let the snake go forth with its body cast off;
let him who seeks merit release it from its bond.
I give you a hundred coins, hunter.
And a large jeweled earring,
and a four-legged couch resembling the color of an *umā* flower.
Two wives of equal status,
a bull, and a hundred cows—
let the serpent go forth with body cast off.
“May he who seeks merit be released from his bonds.
“O Lord of Men, even without a gift,
at your word we shall release this serpent from its bonds.”
"Let the serpent with its body cast loose go forth;
let him who seeks merit be released from bondage.
Thus was the Campeyya Nāga liberated.
He said this to the king:
“Homage to you, O King of Kāsi;
homage to you, O Increaser of Kāsi!”
"I raise my hands in reverence to you;
may I see my own home.
"Truly, they say this is difficult to trust," [he replied].
That a human should place trust in one who is not human—
if you ask me for this purpose,
O Naga, we shall show you our dwellings.
“Even if the wind were to blow away the mountain,
and the moon and sun were to fall to the ground,
and all rivers were to flow upstream, [the Tathāgata’s words would not be otherwise].”
But I would never speak a falsehood, O King,
even if the sky were to split asunder, the ocean were to dry up,
or the earth, the sustainer of beings, were to be overturned.
“Mount Meru, the accumulation of rock,
might rise up together with its roots, but I, O King, would never speak a falsehood.
“For they say that such a thing is indeed beyond belief.”
That a human should place trust in a non-human—
since you ask me for this matter,
O Naga, let us behold your dwellings.
You were once fierce-venomed and formidable,
possessing great power and quick to anger;
yet you were released from bondage without cause.
"You ought not to know what has been done.
"He will surely fall into a terrible hell;
do not obtain even the slightest bodily pleasure."
“Let death come to him who is bound in a basket,
he who does not know such a deed as this was done!
Let this be your word of truth.”
Be free from anger and free from malice;
may all the families of nāgas and supaṇṇas avoid you,
as one avoids fire in the summer heat.
“O Lord of Men, you have compassion for the nāga clan,
just as a mother feels for her own beloved only son;
and I, together with the nāga clan, [revere you].”
“I shall perform a noble service.
“Harness, then, the royal chariots, well-adorned,
with the well-trained, thoroughbred horses from Kamboja.”
"Let them harness the elephants with golden trappings;
let us behold the dwellings of the elephant.
The kettledrums, tabors, cymbals, and conchs—
They honored King Uggasena; King Pāyāsi, appearing most resplendent,
was preceded [by his retinue] in the midst of a throng of women.
Kāsivaḍḍhana beheld the ground strewn with golden heaps and palaces made of gold.
Spread with slabs of beryl,
the king entered the celestial mansion,
the residence of Campeyya.
Resembling the color of the sun,
radiant like bronze lightning,
it was completely covered with various kinds of trees.
Fanned by various fragrances,
that King of Kāsi entered the residence of the Lord of Campā.
When the King of Kāsi had entered the residence of Campeyya,
divine musical instruments resounded.
And the Naga maidens danced.
The King of Kasi, full of faith, followed that performance of the Naga maidens in a great throng.
He sat upon a golden throne,
provided with a cushion of antelope skin and anointed with the essence of sandalwood.
Having eaten there and likewise enjoyed himself, he—
The King of Kāsi said to Campeyyaka:
"These most excellent palaces of yours are radiant, with the color of the sun."
"There are leaders such as these in the world of men;
longing for what, O Naga, do you perform these austerities?
[There are those] wearing shell-bracelets and armlets, well-clothed..."
With rounded fingers and copper-colored palms,
those of extraordinary beauty take hold and feed him;
there is nothing like this in the world of men.
"O Naga, aspiring for what do you perform this asceticism?
Here are rivers with broad-scaled fish,
bathing-places echoing with the cries of waterfowl and birds."
There are such leaders as these in the world of men;
longing for what, O Naga, do you perform this asceticism?
There are curlews, peacocks, and divine swans.
Cuckoos fly about with melodious voices;
there is nothing like this in the world of humans.
O Naga, for what purpose do you perform these austerities?
The ambā trees, the sālās, the tilakas, the jambus,
the uddālakas, and the pāṭalis are in full bloom;
there is nothing like these in the world of men.
"O Nāga, aspiring for what do you perform this asceticism?
For from all around these lotus ponds,
divine fragrances are constantly wafting forth."
“There is no leader such as this in the world of men;
for what purpose, O Naga, do you perform these austerities?
“Neither for the sake of a son, nor for the sake of wealth,”
Nor for the sake of long life,
O Lord of Men; desiring the human womb,
therefore I exert myself and practice austerity.”
“You, with blood-red eyes and broad chest,
adorned and with hair and beard trimmed,
well-anointed with red sandalwood— ”
Like a king of the gandharvas, you illuminate the quarters.
You have attained divine power, O one of great majesty,
and are endowed with all sensual pleasures.
“I ask you this matter, O King of Nagas:
by what is the world of humans superior to this?
“O Lord of Men, there is nothing other than the world of humans [that is superior].”
“Purity or self-restraint indeed exists;
having now obtained this human birth,
I shall bring an end to birth and death.”
“Truly, those who are wise and deeply learned, who reflect upon many matters, should indeed be served;
as should women, and yourself, O Naga.”
“I shall perform abundant meritorious deeds.
“Truly, those who are wise,
learned, and who contemplate many matters, should indeed be served.”
“O King, seeing these women and me,
perform abundant meritorious deeds.
“And this gold of mine is plentiful;”
A heap of gold as high as a palm tree—
having taken this gold from here,
build golden houses and let them construct a silver rampart.
Let five thousand loads of pearls mixed with beryl be brought from here and spread upon the ground within the inner palace.
It shall be free from dust and stainless.
Dwell in such a place, O best of kings,
this most excellent mansion, so exceedingly radiant.
"Bārāṇasī is a city prosperous and flourishing;
rule the kingdom, O you of peerless wisdom!
Thus ends the tenth Jātaka, the Campeyya Jātaka.
